title: Debugging clinic
text: Errors are a normal part of programming. This part presents a method to diagnose them, the most frequent error messages in Stata, and the organisation of a project that can be reproduced by a third party.

title: Debugging clinic
text:
Read the error message
When a command fails, Stata prints a message in red followed by a return code, for instance r(111). The execution of the do-file stops at this line. The message and the code identify the problem.








Code
Message
Frequent cause




r(3)
no dataset in use
No data loaded, or clear all executed before the command


r(9)
assertion is false
A check written with assert failed


r(100)
varlist required
A command requiring variables receives an empty list, for instance from an empty local macro


r(109)
type mismatch
A string variable is compared with a number, or the reverse


r(110)
variable already defined
generate used on an existing name. Use replace or capture drop


r(111)
variable not found
Typo, wrong case (Stata is case sensitive), wrong dataset in memory


r(198)
invalid syntax
Missing comma, misspelt option, unbalanced parenthesis or quotation mark


r(199)
unrecognized command
Misspelt command, or package not installed


r(459)
variable does not uniquely identify observations
Failed isid or merge on a key with duplicates


r(601)
file not found
Wrong path or file name


r(602)
file already exists
save or export without the option replace


r(2000)
no observations
The if condition selects nothing



The description of a return code is obtained with search r(111).

title: Debugging clinic
text:
A method

Read the message and identify the line that failed
Isolate the problem. Execute the code line by line and comment out what is not needed
Inspect the state of the data at the point of failure, with describe, list in 1/5, summarize, tabulate, missing or display
Simplify. Reproduce the error on a built-in dataset, with the smallest possible code
Trace. When the error is inside a loop or a program, set trace on prints each line executed and set trace off stops it. The option set tracedepth 1 limits the level of detail
Search in the documentation with help and search. Then look for the exact message online, for instance on Statalist

* Inspect the value of a local inside a loop
foreach v of varlist price mpg {
    display "Current variable: `v'"
    summarize `v'
}

capture
The prefix capture suppresses the error and stores its return code in _rc.
capture confirm variable price
if _rc != 0 {
    display "The variable price does not exist"
}
capture is appropriate when a failure is expected, for instance capture drop varname before a generate. It should not be used to silence errors that are not understood, since the code then continues on a wrong state.

title: Debugging clinic
text:
Silent errors
The most dangerous errors do not produce any message. The result is wrong but the code runs. The following are the most frequent.

Missing values treated as large numbers in comparisons (see Part 0 and Part 1)
A local macro that is empty, so that summarize `vars' summarises all variables
A merge that does not match all observations, or m:m
A replace with a condition that is more general than intended
A sample that changes between two regressions because of missing values. The number of observations should be compared across columns of a table

Systematic checks limit these risks: assert, isid, count, tabulate, missing, misstable summarize.

title: Debugging clinic
text:
Exercise
Each block below contains one error. For each of them, predict the message, run the code and correct it.






TipExercise



* Block 1
sysuse auto, clear
regress price Mpg

* Block 2
summarize price, detials

* Block 3
generate price = price / 1000

* Block 4
keep if foreign == "Foreign"

* Block 5
save "$path/temp/auto_clean.dta"
save "$path/temp/auto_clean.dta"

* Block 6 (no error message: what is wrong?)
sysuse auto, clear
generate good_record = rep78 > 3
tabulate good_record rep78, missing

* Block 7 (run the two lines separately: what is wrong?)
local vars price mpg
summarize `vars'








NoteSolution






r(111). The variable is mpg. Stata is case sensitive
r(198). The option is detail
r(110). The variable price exists. Use a new name or replace
r(109). The variable foreign is numeric. The condition is foreign == 1. The label is printed by tabulate but is not the value
r(602) at the second line. Add the option replace
The variable rep78 has missing values, which are coded as larger than 3. The observations with a missing repair record are assigned good_record = 1. The correct code is generate good_record = rep78 > 3 if !missing(rep78)
When the lines are executed separately, the local vars does not exist in the second execution. The command summarize with an empty list summarises all the variables and no error is displayed

title: Debugging clinic
text:
Reproducibility
A project is reproducible if a third party can obtain all the results from the raw data, by running one file. This is required by most economics journals and is, above all, the best protection for the author against errors.

Master do-file
The master do-file defines the environment, installs the packages and runs the scripts in order. It is the only file that has to be modified to run the project on another computer.
/*==========================================================================
    MASTER DO-FILE
    Project : Introduction to Stata
    Purpose : Run all the scripts in order
==========================================================================*/

clear all
set more off
set varabbrev off
version 17                 // Oldest version supported. It must not exceed the installed one
capture log close

* ===== 1. Paths =====

* The only lines to modify: one line per user
if "`c(username)'" == "mmoglia" {
    global path "C:/Users/mmoglia/courses/2026_eco51423ep"
}
else if "`c(username)'" == "student" {
    global path "C:/Users/student/courses/2026_eco51423ep"
}

global code   "$path/code"
global raw    "$path/raw_data"
global temp   "$path/temp"
global output "$path/output"
global logs   "$path/logs"

* ===== 2. Run =====

log using "$logs/master.smcl", replace

do "$code/0_install_packages.do"
do "$code/1_clean_data.do"
do "$code/2_merge_datasets.do"
do "$code/3_analysis.do"

log close


Rules

All paths are built from $path, none is written in full in the scripts
The raw data are never modified. Every transformation is performed by a script
Each script starts from the data it needs and does not depend on the state left by another script in memory
The scripts are numbered in the order of execution
Randomness is controlled with set seed. Commands involving random draws, such as sample, start from a sorted dataset, so that the result does not depend on the initial order
The installed packages and the version are documented (about, ado dir, which estout)
A README file describes the folder structure, the sources of the data and the order of execution

set seed 20260928
sort id            // Requires a variable id
sample 10          // Keep 10% of the observations

title: Debugging clinic
text:
Further resources

The Stata documentation, accessible from help and in PDF
Statalist, the reference forum. Search before posting
The Stata Journal and the Stata Tips
The DIME Analytics Data Handbook of the World Bank
The Library of Statistical Translation, which gives equivalent code in Stata, R and Python
The UCLA OARC Stata resources

title: Data visualisation
text: This part covers the main graph types in Stata. Part of the material is adapted from this Princeton tutorial. Variable names of the online datasets follow the original files and should be checked with describe.

title: Data visualisation
text:
General remarks
The standard syntax of a graph command is graph_command variable, options. Several plots are overlaid with twoway, for instance a bar chart and a line, or a scatter plot and a fitted line:
twoway (graph_command1 var1, options1) (graph_command2 var2, options2), general_options
twoway can be abbreviated tw. The options placed inside a parenthesis apply to one plot. The options placed after the last parenthesis apply to the whole graph.
Good practice for graphs:

Label the axes with the variable and its unit
Include a legend when several series are shown, and omit it otherwise
Keep one message per graph and limit the amount of information
Use colours that remain readable in black and white and for colour-blind readers


Schemes
A scheme defines the general look of a graph. The list of official schemes is documented here. The package blindschemes adds schemes with colour-blind safe palettes, such as plotplain and plottig.
ssc install blindschemes, replace
set scheme plotplain


Export
A graph is exported with graph export. The vector format .pdf is preferred for LaTeX documents.
graph export "$path/output/figures/my_graph.pdf", replace
graph export "$path/output/figures/my_graph.png", replace width(2000)

title: Data visualisation
text:
Scatter plots
The command is scatter, abbreviated sc. It requires two variables, y then x, in this order. We use trade data for the year 2012.
use "https://dss.princeton.edu/training/wdipol.dta", clear
keep if year == 2012

scatter import export            // Levels: the graph is hardly readable

generate limport = log(import)   // Logarithms improve readability
generate lexport = log(export)
We now choose the colour, the symbol and the width of the symbol, and label the axes.
scatter limport lexport, ///
    mcolor(cranberry) msymbol(Oh) mlwidth(0.1) ///
    xtitle("Exports (USD, log)") ytitle("Imports (USD, log)")
The same graph with abbreviated options:
sc limport lexport, mc(cranberry) m(Oh) mlw(0.1) xti("Exports (USD, log)") yti("Imports (USD, log)")
Abbreviations are convenient when exploring the data. Complete options are preferred in a do-file.
Markers can be labelled with the option mlabel(). The labels are readable only for a small number of observations.
scatter limport lexport if inlist(country, "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Spain"), ///
    mcolor(cranberry) mlabel(country) mlabposition(3)






TipExercise



Starting from the scatter plot of limport on lexport, add a regression line.

Overlay a second plot with (lfit y x)
Give the line the same colour as the points
Adapt the legend with the option order(), and place it at the bottom









NoteSolution





twoway (scatter limport lexport, mcolor(cranberry) msymbol(Oh) mlwidth(0.1)) ///
       (lfit limport lexport, lcolor(cranberry)), ///
    xtitle("Exports (USD, log)") ytitle("Imports (USD, log)") ///
    legend(pos(6) cols(2) order(1 "Countries" 2 "Linear fit"))
The option pos(6) places the legend at 6 o’clock, that is, below the graph. The order of the plots in the command determines their number in order().

title: Data visualisation
text:
Histograms and bar charts

Histograms
Histograms are produced with histogram, abbreviated hist. We use the full panel of countries.
use "https://dss.princeton.edu/training/wdipol.dta", clear

hist gdppc
hist gdppc, frequency
hist gdppc, kdensity
hist gdppc, kdensity normal
The legend of this latter graph is hardly customisable. Building the graph with twoway gives full control. The global histopts groups the options of the histogram.
global histopts "bin(20) fcolor(ebblue%60) lcolor(white)"

quietly summarize gdppc, detail
local mu = r(mean)
local sigma = r(sd)
local lo = r(p1)
local hi = r(p99)

twoway (hist gdppc, $histopts) ///
       (kdensity gdppc, lcolor(cranberry)) ///
       (function y = normalden(x, `mu', `sigma'), range(`lo' `hi') lcolor(navy)), ///
    xtitle("GDP per capita (USD)") ///
    legend(pos(6) cols(2) order(2 "Kernel density" 3 "Normal distribution"))
The distributions of two groups are compared by overlaying two histograms, with the alternative || syntax of twoway. Here, we compare the distribution of GDP per capita across countries in 1990 and in 2012.
twoway hist gdppc if year == 1990, bin(10) || ///
       hist gdppc if year == 2012, bin(10) fcolor(none) lcolor(red) ///
    legend(label(1 "1990") label(2 "2012"))


Bar charts
The command graph bar (vertical) and graph hbar (horizontal) plot statistics of a variable. The syntax over() plots a statistic for each category of a variable.
sysuse auto, clear
graph bar (mean) price, over(foreign)
We now plot the GDP per capita of the wealthier countries. The selection is based on the average over the period. A selection based on gdppc > 18000 would instead select observations, not countries.
use "https://dss.princeton.edu/training/wdipol.dta", clear

bysort country: egen gdppc_avg = mean(gdppc)

graph hbar (mean) gdppc if gdppc_avg > 18000, ///
    over(country, sort(1) descending label(labsize(*0.7))) ///
    bar(1, color(ebblue))

graph hbar (mean) gdppc (median) gdppc if gdppc_avg > 18000, ///
    over(country, sort(1) descending label(labsize(*0.8))) ///
    legend(label(1 "Mean") label(2 "Median")) ///
    bar(1, color(navy)) bar(2, color(cranberry))

title: Data visualisation
text:
Box plots
generate lgdppc = log(gdppc)
generate ltrade = log(trade)

graph box lgdppc ltrade






TipExercise



Make a box plot with the variables of your choice, for instance the logarithm of imports and exports.

Read carefully the help of graph box
Change the colour of the two boxes
Change the width of the graph with the options xsize() and ysize()
Place the legend below, on two columns
Add a title in bold, using the syntax {bf: text}

title: Data visualisation
text:
Line charts
Line charts are appropriate for time series and panel data. The years are on the x-axis and the values on the y-axis. We use the built-in life expectancy dataset.
sysuse uslifeexp, clear

line le year                        // The variable on the y-axis is placed first
line le_male le_female year         // Several series: the x variable is always last
An alternative uses scatter with the option connect().
scatter le_male le_female year, connect(l l) msymbol(none none)
We improve the graph in three ways: the legend is placed inside the plot region, the lines are restyled and an annotation is added. We first change the legend and the titles.
line le_male le_female year, ///
    legend(ring(0) pos(5) region(lstyle(none))) ///
    title("{bf:Life expectancy} in the 20th century") ///
    xtitle("Year") ytitle("Years") ///
    note("Source: US Census Bureau") ///
    ylabel(, nogrid) xlabel(, nogrid)
The option ring(0) places the legend inside the plot region and pos(5) at 5 o’clock. The grid is removed by nogrid and the title is in bold thanks to {bf: }.
The lines are restyled with lcolor() and lpattern():
line le_male le_female year, ///
    lcolor(green cranberry) lpattern(longdash longdash_dot) ///
    legend(ring(0) pos(5) region(lstyle(none))) ///
    title("{bf:Life expectancy} in the 20th century") ///
    xtitle("Year") ytitle("Years") ///
    note("Source: US Census Bureau") ///
    ylabel(, nogrid) xlabel(, nogrid)
The drop of life expectancy in 1918 is due to the Spanish flu. We add an arrow with pcarrowi y1 x1 y2 x2 (clockposition) "label". It goes from the point \((x_1, y_1)\) to the point \((x_2, y_2)\).
twoway (line le_male le_female year, ///
            lcolor(green cranberry) lpattern(longdash longdash_dot)) ///
       (pcarrowi 45 1930 40 1918 (2) "Spanish flu", ///
            color(black) mlabcolor(black)), ///
    legend(order(1 2) ring(0) pos(5) region(lstyle(none))) ///
    title("{bf:Life expectancy} in the 20th century") ///
    xtitle("Year") ytitle("Years") ///
    note("Source: US Census Bureau") ///
    ylabel(, nogrid) xlabel(, nogrid)
The option order(1 2) keeps only the two lines in the legend and excludes the arrow.

title: Data visualisation
text:
Regression coefficients
Regression coefficients are plotted with their confidence intervals using the package coefplot. Part of the material is adapted from this blog post.
ssc install coefplot, replace
We use the auto dataset. The variables are rescaled between 0 and 1, so that their coefficients are comparable. A loop avoids repeating the same code.
sysuse auto, clear

foreach v in mpg weight length {
    quietly summarize `v'
    generate `v'_01 = (`v' - r(min)) / (r(max) - r(min))
}
A standardised variable (mean 0 and standard deviation 1) is obtained with egen mpg_std = std(mpg).
We run a regression and plot its coefficients. coefplot uses the last estimation by default.
regress price mpg_01 weight_01 length_01 i.foreign, vce(robust)
coefplot






Tip



Estimates stored with eststo can be used directly: coefplot m1. They can be restored with estimates restore m1, which is also useful to access the e() results.


The graph is improved step by step. The names of the coefficients are printed by regress, coeflegend.
regress, coeflegend      // Print the names to use in the options of coefplot

* Vertical line at zero and removal of the constant
global coefplotopts "drop(_cons) xline(0, lcolor(red) lwidth(medium))"

coefplot, $coefplotopts ///
    coeflabels(mpg_01 = "MPG" weight_01 = "Weight" length_01 = "Length")

* A more complete model
regress price mpg_01 weight_01 length_01 i.foreign i.foreign#c.mpg_01, vce(robust)

coefplot, $coefplotopts ///
    coeflabels(mpg_01 = "MPG" weight_01 = "Weight" length_01 = "Length" ///
               1.foreign = "Foreign" 1.foreign#c.mpg_01 = "MPG X Foreign")

* Final version
coefplot, $coefplotopts ///
    xtitle("{bf:Effect on vehicle price (USD)}") ///
    graphregion(margin(medsmall)) ///
    xlabel(, nogrid) ///
    ylabel(, glpattern(dash) glcolor(gs14)) ///
    coeflabels(mpg_01 = "MPG" length_01 = "Length" weight_01 = "Weight" ///
               1.foreign = "Foreign" 1.foreign#c.mpg_01 = `""MPG X" "Foreign""') ///
    headings(mpg_01 = "{bf:Vehicle specs}" ///
             1.foreign = "{bf:Production info}" ///
             1.foreign#c.mpg_01 = "{bf:Interactions}", gap(0))
Several models are compared in the same graph. Each model is stored and passed in a parenthesis, with its own label.
eststo clear
eststo m1: regress price mpg_01 weight_01 length_01, vce(robust)
eststo m2: regress price mpg_01 weight_01 length_01 i.foreign, vce(robust)

coefplot (m1, label("Baseline")) (m2, label("With origin")), ///
    keep(mpg_01 weight_01 length_01) xline(0) legend(pos(6) cols(2))
The confidence level is chosen with levels(), and several levels are plotted at once with levels(95 90).

title: Data visualisation
text:
Exercise
Does trade orientation correlate with life expectancy? We use the dataset wdipol and a World Bank dataset on male life expectancy.






TipExercise



Life expectancy data

Download, save and open the World Bank dataset. The archive contains a .csv file with header lines. Open it with import delimited and inspect the first rows with browse
Keep the country names and the variables whose name starts with v, except the last one, which is empty
Using a loop, rename the v variables into le_maleYYYY
Reshape to long format with a new column year
Save as a temporary file

Hints for steps 1 to 4. The years are stored in the labels of the variables v. The following pieces of code can be adapted.
* The row containing the column headers (here 5) must be checked in the file
import delimited "$path/raw_data/API_SP.DYN.LE00.MA.IN.csv", varnames(5) clear
rename countryname country

foreach v of varlist v* {
    local yr : variable label `v'
    if "`yr'" == "" drop `v'
    else rename `v' le_male`yr'
}

reshape long le_male, i(country) j(year)
By now, the dataset should look as follows:
. list in 1/10

     +------------------------------+
     |     country   year   le_male |
     |------------------------------|
  1. | Afghanistan   1960    32.136 |
  2. | Afghanistan   1961    32.626 |
  3. | Afghanistan   1962    33.098 |
  4. | Afghanistan   1963    33.543 |
  5. | Afghanistan   1964    34.004 |
     |------------------------------|
  6. | Afghanistan   1965    34.438 |
  7. | Afghanistan   1966    34.877 |
  8. | Afghanistan   1967    35.324 |
  9. | Afghanistan   1968    35.825 |
 10. | Afghanistan   1969    36.287 |
     +------------------------------+
Trade data

Open the trade data and keep country, year, export and import
Compute the export share xshare, defined as export / (export + import)
Drop the observations with a missing export share
Merge with the life expectancy data (1:1, with country and year as keys)
Keep the matched observations only
Count the number of observations by country (hint: bysort country: generate count = _N)
Using a local, keep only the countries observed in all years of the panel

By now, the dataset should look as follows:
     +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
     | year     country      export      import    xshare   le_male        _merge   count |
     |-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
  1. | 1980   Australia   32720.597    26890.83   .548898     70.88   Matched (3)      33 |
  2. | 1981   Australia   31132.097   29423.028  .5141117      71.2   Matched (3)      33 |
  3. | 1982   Australia    31867.06   32823.251  .4926095      71.5   Matched (3)      33 |
  4. | 1983   Australia   32032.664   30058.226  .5158996      71.8   Matched (3)      33 |
  5. | 1984   Australia   34477.203   31856.781  .5197517      72.1   Matched (3)      33 |
     +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
The export share is not the usual measure of trade openness, which is the sum of exports and imports over GDP. It is used here for simplicity.
Continents
We compute summary statistics by continent. Define the following globals. Text is enclosed in compound quotation marks when it contains commas.
global europe  "Austria Belgium Bulgaria Denmark Finland France Greece Italy Luxembourg Netherlands Norway Portugal Sweden"
global oceania "Australia"
global asia    "Bangladesh India Indonesia Jordan Malaysia Pakistan Philippines Singapore Thailand"
global africa  `" "Congo, Dem. Rep." "Congo, Rep." "Kenya" "Lesotho" "Mauritania" "Mauritius" "Morocco" "Mozambique" "Rwanda" "South Africa" "Tunisia" "'
global latam   `" "Bolivia" "Brazil" "Chile" "Colombia" "Costa Rica" "Dominican Republic" "Ecuador" "El Salvador" "Guatemala" "Honduras" "Mexico" "Nicaragua" "Panama" "Peru" "Uruguay" "'

Using loops over the globals, fill a variable continent with the name of the continent
Save as a temporary file

It should look as follows:
. list country continent in 1/10, compress

     +----------------------+
     |   country  continent |
     |----------------------|
  1. | Australia    Oceania |
  2. | Australia    Oceania |
  ...
Graphs

Make a scatter plot of life expectancy and export share in 2012
Make a scatter plot with the two years 1980 and 2012 on the same graph
Using lfitci, add a confidence interval to the first plot. In the legend, keep only the linear fit and the points. Add the note “95% confidence interval” below the graph
Export the graph as .pdf

We now compute and plot the mean of life expectancy and of the export share by continent and year.

Use preserve and restore to keep the main dataset in memory during the exercise
Collapse life expectancy and export share by continent and year, with the mean and the median
With a two-axis plot, show the evolution of the export share and of life expectancy for Asia
Make a plot with one panel per continent showing the same relationship (option by(continent))

Regressions

Regress life expectancy on the export share with the option vce(robust)
Add a dummy for each continent. What must be done first?
Add year dummies
Plot the coefficients of the last regression for the export share and the continent dummies only
Plot the coefficients of the export share across the three regressions









NoteHints for the graphs and regressions





* Confidence interval: lfitci draws the interval (plot 1), the line (plot 2)
twoway (lfitci le_male xshare) (scatter le_male xshare), ///
    legend(order(3 "Countries" 2 "Linear fit")) note("95% confidence interval")

* Two axes: each series is attached to one axis
twoway (line xshare year, yaxis(1)) (line le_male year, yaxis(2)), ///
    ytitle("Export share", axis(1)) ytitle("Life expectancy (years)", axis(2)) ///
    legend(order(1 "Export share" 2 "Life expectancy"))

* Continent dummies: the string variable must be encoded first
encode continent, generate(continent_id)
regress le_male xshare i.continent_id, vce(robust)

* Coefficients across models
eststo clear
eststo m1: regress le_male xshare, vce(robust)
eststo m2: regress le_male xshare i.continent_id, vce(robust)
eststo m3: regress le_male xshare i.continent_id i.year, vce(robust)
coefplot m1 m2 m3, keep(xshare) xline(0)

title: Data manipulation
text: This part covers the core data management tasks: opening files, cleaning and creating variables, using macros and loops, reshaping datasets and combining them. We use built-in Stata datasets and a small number of online files.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Open and save data
The built-in datasets are opened with sysuse. Other formats require the following commands.
* Built-in datasets
sysuse auto, clear

* Stata format (.dta)
use "$path/raw_data/mydata.dta", clear

* Excel files
import excel "$path/raw_data/mydata.xlsx", sheet("Sheet1") firstrow clear

* Delimited files (.csv, .txt)
import delimited "$path/raw_data/mydata.csv", delimiter(",") varnames(1) clear

* Files available online
use "https://www.stata.com/users/youtube/rawdata.dta", clear

* Save the dataset in memory
save "$path/temp/mydata_clean.dta", replace






Tip



Stata does not overwrite the data in memory by default. The option clear is required to load a dataset when another one is already open. Similarly, save requires the option replace to overwrite an existing file.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Describe the data
For this section, we use the dataset rawdata.dta, which contains health information on individuals. The variable names follow the original file. They should be checked with describe before use.






TipExercise



Open a do-file, start with clear all and follow the instructions:

Open the file rawdata.dta with the link above
Use browse to inspect the data
Use describe to inspect the format of the variables
Use count to print the number of observations
Use tabulate to print a frequency table for sex
Use summarize to print summary statistics for the cholesterol concentration (chol). What is the issue?

title: Data manipulation
text:
Data cleaning
The dataset requires cleaning. We proceed step by step.

Keep and drop
Assume that we keep individuals aged more than 25, which is equivalent to dropping those aged 25 or less.
keep if age > 25 & !missing(age)
* Equivalent: drop if age <= 25 | missing(age)






WarningMissing values



In Stata, a missing value is larger than any number. Without the condition !missing(age), the command keep if age > 25 retains the observations with a missing age. The same rule applies to generate and replace with inequalities (see below).


Observations with a missing date of birth are dropped. The sample is then restricted to two racial groups.
drop if missing(dob)
keep if inlist(race, "White", "Black")
* Equivalent if "Other" is the only other category: drop if race == "Other"


Change the format of a variable
The cholesterol concentration is stored as a string and should be numeric. Before converting, we identify the entries that prevent the conversion.
list chol if missing(real(chol)) & !missing(chol)   // Non-numeric entries
destring chol, replace                              // Convert in place
destring chol, generate(chol_num)                   // Or create a new variable
The related commands are tostring (numeric to string), encode (string to labelled numeric) and decode (labelled numeric to string).


Variable labels and value labels
A variable label describes a variable. A value label describes the values of a categorical variable. Some variables of the dataset have no label. Using label variable, we label age and dob.
label variable age "Age (years)"
label variable dob "Date of birth"
The variable sex takes the values 0 (female) and 1 (male). To print these names instead of the numbers, we define a value label and attach it to the variable.
label define sex_lab 0 "Female" 1 "Male"
label values sex sex_lab

tabulate sex        // Check
tabulate sex, nolabel   // Display the underlying values


Create variables
The command generate creates a variable and replace modifies an existing one. We build a dummy variable for race.
generate race_dummy = .                   // Create an empty variable
replace race_dummy = 1 if race == "White"
replace race_dummy = 0 if race == "Black"
A dummy variable can also be created in one line. The comparison returns 1 if true and 0 otherwise.
generate white = (race == "White") if !missing(race)


Grouping variable 1: bins
The cholesterol concentration is heterogeneous:
. summarize chol

    Variable |        Obs        Mean    Std. dev.       Min        Max
-------------+---------------------------------------------------------
        chol |      1,266    216.4415    46.84972         89        426
We want to assign each individual to a bin of width 10, identified by its lower bound. Two approaches exist, a built-in function and a loop. Note that round(chol, 10) would assign the nearest multiple of 10, which is different.
* Built-in function
generate floored_chol = floor(chol/10)*10
* Loop
generate floored_chol_loop = .
forvalues x = 80(10)420 {
    replace floored_chol_loop = `x' if chol >= `x' & chol < `x' + 10
}
The loop is read as follows:

generate creates an empty numeric variable
forvalues x = 80(10)420 { opens a loop where the running variable x goes from 80 to 420 with a step of 10
replace assigns the value x to the observations whose chol lies in the interval \([x, x+10)\)
} closes the loop. The brace { must be the last character of the first line and } must be alone on its line.

Two remarks:

The function inrange(chol, x, x + 9) is inclusive on both sides. Why is it inappropriate when chol is not an integer?
Which of the two approaches is the most efficient? When is a loop justified?



Grouping variable 2: comparison with the mean
We want a variable equal to 1 if the weight is above the mean and 0 otherwise.






TipExercise



Create the variable in three steps:

Compute the mean of weight
Generate a variable containing this mean, with egen new_var = mean(var)
Generate the dummy variable. Pay attention to missing values.









NoteSolution





egen weight_mean = mean(weight)
generate weight_above = (weight > weight_mean) if !missing(weight)
A shorter version using stored results is presented in the next section.





Grouping variable 3: statistics by group
We now want to identify individuals whose cholesterol concentration exceeds the 3rd quartile of their own age class. The prefix by computes a statistic within groups. It is used in two ways:

As a prefix, after sorting: bysort age_class: command. The prefix is equivalent to by age_class, sort: command.
As an option, for the commands that allow it: egen ..., by(age_class).

The prefix is more general and works with most commands.






TipExercise




Create the variable age_class, equal to the lower bound of the decade of age
Compute the 75th percentile of chol within each age class, with egen and the function pctile()
Create the dummy chol_high, equal to 1 if chol is above this threshold









NoteSolution





generate age_class = floor(age/10)*10
bysort age_class: egen chol_p75 = pctile(chol), p(75)
generate chol_high = (chol > chol_p75) if !missing(chol)
tabulate age_class chol_high, row

title: Data manipulation
text:
Stored results, locals and globals
Three objects should not be confused.
Stored results. After most commands, Stata stores results in memory. The results of descriptive commands are r() and those of estimation commands are e(). They are listed with return list and ereturn list. They are overwritten by the next command of the same class.
Local macros. A local macro is a named piece of text. It is defined with local and called between a backtick and an apostrophe, `name'. It exists only during the current execution of the do-file.
Global macros. A global macro is defined with global and called with $name (or ${name}). It persists until Stata is closed.
quietly summarize weight
return list                                  // Results stored by summarize

generate weight_above2 = (weight > r(mean)) if !missing(weight)

local threshold = r(mean)                    // Copy a stored result in a local
display "Mean weight: `threshold'"






WarningExecution of locals



A local macro disappears when the execution ends. If a do-file is run by selecting and executing lines separately, each execution is independent. A local defined in the first execution is empty in the second one. The command then fails, or worse, runs silently on an empty argument. Blocks that use locals must be selected and executed together.


Stored results can also be used in the loop presented above, which then adapts to the range of the data:
use "https://www.stata.com/users/youtube/rawdata.dta", clear
destring chol, replace

capture drop floored_chol
generate floored_chol = .

quietly summarize chol
local min_chol = floor(r(min)/10)*10
local max_chol = ceil(r(max)/10)*10
local step = 10

forvalues x = `min_chol'(`step')`max_chol' {
    quietly replace floored_chol = `x' if chol >= `x' & chol < `x' + `step'
}
Globals store information for a longer period. The path of the working directory is the typical example.
global path "C:/Users/username/courses/2026_eco51423ep"
global sexes "Male Female"

use "$path/raw_data/mydata.dta", clear
Text macros are defined without the sign =. With =, Stata evaluates an expression, which imposes a length limit on strings.

title: Data manipulation
Data manipulation
text:
Strings and dates
String variables are frequent in raw data. In the health dataset, the date of birth is stored as a string. We first inspect the format.
list dob in 1/5
The following functions are used to extract elements of a string.
generate month3 = strupper(substr(dob, 1, 3))     // First three letters, upper case
generate first_word = word(dob, 1)                // First word
generate first_word2 = substr(dob, 1, strpos(dob, " ") - 1)   // Equivalent

substr(s, n1, n2) returns n2 characters starting at position n1. The third argument is a length, not an end position.
strpos(s, t) returns the position of the string t in s, and 0 if it is absent.
word(s, n) returns the nth word, words being separated by spaces.
Other useful functions: strlen, strtrim, strlower, subinstr, regexm. The command split separates a string into several variables.

A date stored as a string cannot be used in computations. It is converted with date() and displayed with a date format. The mask (here MDY) must match the format of the string.
generate dob_date = date(dob, "MDY")
format dob_date %td
generate birth_year = year(dob_date)

title: Data manipulation
text:
Reshape, collapse, merge and append
For this section, we use the built-in dataset uslifeexp.dta. It contains, for each year, the life expectancy of the overall population (le), and by gender, race and gender-race.

Reshape
The dataset is in wide format: each row is a year and each group has its own column. We want a long format, with one row per year and per group. This operation is called reshaping.
sysuse uslifeexp, clear
describe

rename le le_all                 // The overall series must follow the pattern le_*
reshape long le_, i(year) j(group) string
rename le_ le
The syntax is as follows:

reshape long converts from wide to long and reshape wide from long to wide
le_ is the stub, the common beginning of the names of the variables to reshape
i() contains the identifier of the observation, which does not change
j() is the name of the new variable, which contains the suffixes of the variables (here the groups)
string is required if the suffixes contain letters

The dataset now has three columns: year, group and le. The command reshape wide le, i(year) j(group) string reverses the operation.


Collapse
We want the average life expectancy by group and by decade. We create the decade and use collapse.
generate decade = floor(year/10)*10
collapse (mean) le, by(decade group)
collapse replaces the dataset in memory by a dataset of statistics. Other statistics are available: median, sd, count, min, max. Several statistics can be computed at once, for instance collapse (mean) le_mean = le (sd) le_sd = le, by(decade group). The command is destructive and is usually placed between preserve and restore (see below).


Merge
Two datasets are joined with merge. One of them is in memory (the master) and the other is on disk (the using dataset). The syntax is:
merge 1:1 state using "$path/temp/census1980.dta"
The type of merge describes the relation between the observations of the two datasets:

1:1: each key appears at most once in each dataset
m:1: several observations of the master share the same key in the using dataset
1:m: the reverse of m:1
m:m: not to be used. The result is arbitrary and the Stata manual advises against it.

merge creates the variable _merge, which tags the origin of each observation.



Value
Meaning




1
in the master only


2
in the using dataset only


3
in both (matched)



A rigorous merge follows a fixed routine. The uniqueness of the key is checked before the merge and the outcome is verified after.
isid state                                        // Fails if state is not unique
merge 1:1 state using "$path/temp/census1980.dta", gen(merge_census)
tabulate merge_census                             // Inspect the outcome
list state if merge_census != 3                   // Identify the problem
keep if merge_census == 3                         // Or: assert merge_census == 3
drop merge_census
The options keep(match), keepusing(varlist), assert(match) and nogenerate shorten this routine. An exercise on merge is proposed in Part 2.


Append
append stacks two datasets. The variables are matched by name. A variable absent from one dataset is filled with missing values (. for numeric variables and an empty string for string variables).
append using "$path/temp/census2010.dta", generate(source)
The option generate() creates a variable identifying the origin of each observation. Variables with the same name but different types (numeric and string) generate an error.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Temporary datasets
It is sometimes convenient to store a dataset in memory temporarily.

tempfile
A subset of the data is saved in a temporary file, without writing it on the disk, and appended to another one. Temporary files are local macros and the warning above applies: the block is executed as a whole.
use "$path/raw_data/data.dta", clear
drop if gender == 0
* ... cleaning ...

tempfile males
save `males'

use "$path/raw_data/data.dta", clear
drop if gender == 1
* ... cleaning ...

append using `males'


preserve and restore
To compute an intermediary statistic, save it, and go back to the main dataset, the data are preserved and then restored.
sysuse auto, clear

* ... code ...

preserve
collapse (mean) price, by(foreign)
save "$path/temp/price_by_foreign.dta", replace
restore

* ... the code continues on the original dataset ...

title: Data manipulation
text:
Frames
Since Stata 16, several datasets can be held in memory in frames. The dataset opened at the start of a session is in the frame default.
frame create census                                    // Create a frame
frame census: use "$path/temp/census1980.dta", clear   // Load data in it
frames dir                                             // List the frames

frame change census                                    // Move to the frame
frame change default                                   // Come back

* Bring a variable from another frame, without merge
frlink m:1 state, frame(census)
frget pop1980, from(census)

frame drop census
Frames avoid the repeated saving and loading of temporary files. merge remains the standard tool and is the one used in the exercises.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Data quality checks
Checks are included in the do-file, not only performed interactively. A command that fails stops the execution and signals the problem.
isid id                                  // Fails if id does not identify the observations
duplicates report id                     // Number of duplicates
assert age >= 0 & age < 120 if !missing(age)   // Fails if the condition is false
misstable summarize                      // Missing values by variable
codebook, compact                        // Compact description of all variables
compress                                 // Reduce the storage size of the variables

title: Introduction to Stata
text: This website contains the tutorials of the Introduction to Stata course of the Master’s programme at École Polytechnique. The course has three objectives: (i) master the basics of Stata, (ii) implement the standard statistical and empirical tools, and (iii) produce publication-quality output.

title: Introduction to Stata
text:
Conventions used on this website

Code blocks are displayed but not executed. Each block must be copied into a do-file.
Comments in the code start with // or *.
The global macro $path denotes the working directory. It is defined in Part 0.
Some commands come from user-written packages. They are installed once per computer (see Part 0).
Datasets are called by name. Their location is $path/raw_data/.







TipExercise



Exercises appear in boxes of this type.

title: Introduction to Stata
section: About this site and its inspirations
text:
About this site and its inspirations
This site was created for teaching purposes. It is perfectible and any constructive comment is welcome (write me an email). The material draws on the teaching resources listed here.

title: First hand on Stata
text: This part introduces the software, its logic and the working conventions used throughout the course. Stata is proprietary software, first released in 1985. The version used as a reference here is Stata 19.

title: First hand on Stata
text:
General philosophy
Stata works on one active dataset at a time. Every command acts on the dataset held in memory. Since Stata 16, several datasets can be held simultaneously in frames. The one-dataset logic nevertheless remains the default.
Code is written in a do-file, a text file with the extension .do. A do-file can be executed entirely or line by line. Each line is a separate command.
Stata has three main strengths. Its syntax is compact and stable across versions. It is efficient for standard econometric tasks. Tables and figures are easily exported to .tex, .pdf or image formats. Its main limitations are its price and its limited flexibility for non-tabular data.

title: First hand on Stata
text:
The interface







Window
Content




Command
Line where a single command is typed and executed


Results
Output of the commands


Review
History of the commands executed


Variables
Variables of the dataset, with their labels


Properties
Characteristics of the selected variable and of the dataset


Do-file editor
Text editor for scripts, opened with doedit


Data browser and editor
Spreadsheet view of the data, opened with browse or edit









Warning



edit allows manual changes to the data. Manual changes are not recorded in any script and cannot be reproduced. browse is the appropriate command to inspect a dataset.

title: First hand on Stata
text:
Best practice
Some practices should be adopted before writing the first line of code. They matter for three reasons:

Reproducibility is a requirement of empirical research. Most leading economics journals require a replication package.
A structured project reduces errors and facilitates collaboration.
Code is read more often than it is written, including by its author, months later.


Folder organisation
Each project is stored in a working directory (wd), which contains a fixed set of subfolders. The same structure is used in every project. This saves time when navigating between projects or changing computers.
~/courses/2026_eco51423ep/
├── code/          <- do-files
├── raw_data/      <- original data, never modified
├── temp/          <- intermediate datasets
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
└── logs/          <- log files
The folder raw_data is treated as read-only. Every transformation of the data is performed by a do-file and saved in temp.


Naming conventions
File names are short, self-explanatory and written in lower case. Spaces and special characters are avoided. An underscore is used instead. A numeric prefix indicates the order of execution, for instance 1_clean_data.do, 2_merge_datasets.do and 3_analysis.do.
Variables follow the same logic. A dataset of wages for individuals aged 25 to 30 can be called wage_25_30. The name w2530 is too short and wage_individuals_aged_25_30 is too long.


Writing code

Code is commented. The comments explain the purpose of a block, not the syntax of each line.
Comments start with * (at the beginning of a line) or // (after a space, at the end of a line). A block of comments is placed between /* and */.
A long line is split with ///.
Scripts are short and each script has one purpose.
Paths are written with forward slashes (/) on every operating system.

title: First hand on Stata
text:
The do-file
A do-file starts with a header and a set-up block. The following template is used throughout the course.
/*==========================================================================
    Project : Introduction to Stata
    File    : code_tutorial.do
    Author  : First Last
    Date    : 28 September 2026
    Purpose : Load the auto dataset and produce basic descriptive output
==========================================================================*/

* ===== 1. Set-up =====

clear all                 // Empty the memory
set more off              // Do not pause the output
set varabbrev off         // Require complete variable names
capture log close         // Close a possibly open log without error

global path "C:/Users/username/courses/2026_eco51423ep"   // To adapt
cd "$path"

log using "$path/logs/part0.smcl", replace

* ===== 2. Data =====

sysuse auto, clear

* ===== 3. Analysis =====

describe
summarize price mpg weight

log close
The global macro $path is defined once, at the top of the do-file. All the other paths are built from it. To run the code on another computer, only this line is modified.

Run lines
A do-file is executed entirely with Ctrl + D (Shift + Cmd + D on macOS). Selecting some lines before pressing the shortcut executes the selection only.
By default, Stata prints all the output. The prefix quietly suppresses the output of a command. A whole block can be silenced with braces.
quietly summarize price

quietly {
    regress price mpg
    predict price_hat
}
The prefix noisily reactivates the output within a quietly block.


Logs
A log file records the commands and the output displayed in the Results window. It is opened with log using and closed with log close.
capture log close
log using "$path/logs/part0.smcl", replace   // Open a log in the Stata format
log using "$path/logs/part0.log", replace text   // Or a plain text log

* ... commands ...

log close
capture log close at the top of the do-file avoids an error if a log is already open, for instance after an interrupted execution.


Getting help
help summarize        // Documentation of a command
search panel data     // Search by keyword in the documentation and the packages
The complete documentation is available in PDF from the menu Help. The command help is the first reference, before any online search.

title: First hand on Stata
text:
Syntax
The syntax of most Stata commands follows the same structure:
[by varlist:] command [varlist] [if] [in] [weight] [using filename] [, options]
A command starts with its name, for instance summarize. It is followed by the variables (or the object, the path, etc.), by conditions and by options placed after a comma.
sysuse auto, clear

summarize price mpg                      // Two variables
summarize price mpg if foreign == 1      // A condition
summarize price in 1/20                  // The first 20 observations
summarize price, detail                  // An option
bysort foreign: summarize price          // A prefix: one output per group

Abbreviations and wildcards
Most commands have shortcuts. regress can be written reg and summarize can be written su or sum. Options can also be abbreviated. Abbreviations of command names are convenient in the Command window but reduce readability in a do-file.
Abbreviations of variable names are a source of errors. The option set varabbrev off, included in the header above, disables them.
Wildcards are available in lists of variables:

* stands for any string of characters
? stands for exactly one character
- denotes a range of variables, in the order of the dataset

Consider the variables popmun2007, popmun2008, up to popmun2020. To summarise these 14 variables:
summarize popmun2007 popmun2008 popmun2009 popmun2010 popmun2011 popmun2012 popmun2013 popmun2014 popmun2015 popmun2016 popmun2017 popmun2018 popmun2019 popmun2020
summarize popmun2007-popmun2020     // Only if the variables are in that order
summarize popmun*                   // Requires that no other variable starts with popmun


Operators and missing values

Comparison: == (equal to), != (different from), >, >=, <, <=
Logical operators: & (and), | (or), ! (not)
Membership and range: inlist(x, 1, 2, 3) and inrange(x, 10, 20)
Missing values: missing(x) is true if x is missing







WarningMissing values



A missing numeric value is denoted . and is treated by Stata as larger than any number. The condition age > 25 is therefore true for an observation with a missing age. Conditions on variables containing missing values should include & !missing(age). This point causes frequent silent errors and is revisited in Part 1.

title: First hand on Stata
text:
First commands
The following commands describe a dataset. They are run on the built-in auto dataset.
sysuse auto, clear

describe                  // Variables, types, labels
codebook price foreign    // Detailed description of selected variables
list make price in 1/5    // Print observations
summarize price mpg       // Summary statistics
tabulate foreign          // Frequency table
count if foreign == 1     // Number of observations satisfying a condition






TipExercise




Create the folder structure presented above and open a new do-file with the header template.
Define $path and open a log file.
Load the auto dataset. How many observations and variables does it contain?
Compute the mean, the median and the 90th percentile of price.
What is the share of foreign cars?
How many foreign cars are priced above 10,000 USD?
Close the log and open the file in a text editor.









NoteSolution





sysuse auto, clear

describe                              // 74 observations, 12 variables
summarize price, detail               // Mean, median (p50) and p90 in the output
tabulate foreign                      // Share of foreign cars in the Percent column
count if foreign == 1 & price > 10000

title: First hand on Stata
text:
Install packages
A large part of the work can be done with base Stata. Historically, user-written packages have been integrated progressively in the main version. Some packages nevertheless have to be installed beforehand. The installation is done once per computer.
ssc install estout, replace         // Tables (Part 2)
ssc install coefplot, replace       // Coefficient plots (Part 3)
ssc install blindschemes, replace   // Graph schemes (Part 3)
ssc install ftools, replace         // Required by reghdfe (Part 4)
ssc install reghdfe, replace        // High-dimensional fixed effects (Part 4)
To check whether a package is installed, type which estout. The command ssc describe estout prints its description.






Warning



On shared computers, the installed packages may be erased when the session is closed. The installation block is then run at the beginning of each session. It is also part of the master do-file presented in Part 5.

title: Summary statistics
text: This part covers the computation of summary statistics, in particular by group, and their export to LaTeX. It also introduces regression tables.

title: Summary statistics
text:
Simple statistics
We use the standard auto.dta dataset.
sysuse auto, clear

describe
summarize
list in 1/10
Summary statistics for one variable, with and without the detailed distribution:
summarize price
summarize price, detail
The command tabstat is more compact and handles several variables. The option by() splits the statistics by a categorical variable, and statistics() selects the statistics.
tabstat price mpg weight length, statistics(mean sd min p50 max n) columns(statistics)
tabstat price mpg weight, by(foreign) statistics(mean sd p50 n) columns(statistics)
Frequency tables are obtained with tabulate, for one or two variables. Missing values are excluded unless the option missing is specified.
tabulate foreign
tabulate foreign rep78, row column
tabulate foreign rep78, missing
The mean of a variable by category is printed with the option summarize().
tabulate foreign, summarize(mpg)
A test of equality of means between two groups is performed with ttest. The option unequal allows for different variances.
ttest price, by(foreign) unequal
The pairwise correlations are obtained with correlate (listwise deletion) or pwcorr (pairwise deletion, with significance levels).
correlate price mpg weight
pwcorr price mpg weight, sig

title: Summary statistics
text:
LaTeX export
The package estout provides two commands. estpost stores the output of descriptive commands (summarize, tabstat, tabulate, ttest) as estimation results. esttab writes these results in a table, in several formats including LaTeX.






TipInstall packages



The package estout is installed once per computer:
ssc install estout, replace


The key commands are the following.

eststo clear removes the stored estimates, to start from a clean state
estpost stores the results of a descriptive command
esttab prints or exports the table


Overall summary statistics
eststo clear
estpost summarize price mpg weight length, detail listwise

esttab using "$path/output/tables/summary_overall.tex", replace ///
    title("Summary statistics") ///
    cells("count(fmt(%9.0f)) mean(fmt(%9.2f)) sd(fmt(%9.2f)) min(fmt(%9.0f)) p50(fmt(%9.2f)) max(fmt(%9.0f))") ///
    label booktabs noobs nomtitle
The option detail is required for the median (p50) to be stored. The file summary_overall.tex can be included in a LaTeX document with \input{}.






TipLine breaks



The symbol /// at the end of a line indicates that the command continues on the next line. It is required in do-files, whatever the version of Stata. The automatic wrapping displayed in the editor is a visual feature and does not split the command. Since a command spans several lines, the whole block must be selected and executed together.




Summary statistics by group
The table below reports the mean and the standard deviation of price, mpg and weight for each value of foreign.
eststo clear
estpost tabstat price mpg weight, by(foreign) statistics(mean sd p50 n) nototal columns(statistics)

esttab . using "$path/output/tables/summary_by_foreign.tex", replace ///
    cells(mean sd) label nogaps booktabs noobs nomtitle
Other text formats are available: .txt, .csv, .smcl (the Stata format), or .rtf. Excel files are produced with the command putexcel, which is not covered here.
An alternative builds one column per group. It gives full control over the layout.
eststo clear

estpost summarize price mpg weight if foreign == 0
eststo domestic
estpost summarize price mpg weight if foreign == 1
eststo foreign_cars

esttab domestic foreign_cars using "$path/output/tables/summary_groups.tex", replace ///
    cells("mean(fmt(%9.2f)) sd(fmt(%9.2f))") ///
    mtitles("Domestic" "Foreign") label booktabs noobs


Balance table
Economic papers usually report the means of two groups and the test of their difference. The command estpost ttest stores the means of each group (mu_1, mu_2) and the difference (b).
eststo clear
estpost ttest price mpg weight length, by(foreign)

esttab using "$path/output/tables/balance.tex", replace ///
    cells("mu_1(fmt(%9.2f)) mu_2(fmt(%9.2f)) b(star fmt(%9.2f))") ///
    collabels("Domestic" "Foreign" "Difference") ///
    star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) label booktabs noobs nomtitle nonumber
The difference is computed as the mean of the first group minus the mean of the second group. The sign should be checked against the coding of the variable.


Frequency table
eststo clear
estpost tabulate foreign

esttab using "$path/output/tables/freq_foreign.tex", replace ///
    cells("b(label(Frequency)) pct(fmt(%9.2f))") ///
    label booktabs noobs nomtitle

title: Summary statistics
text:
Regression tables
A regression table requires a regression. The syntax is regress y x, options. Many other estimators exist (areg, ivregress, reghdfe, etc.). They depend on the model and are beyond the scope of this part.
We study the correlation between the characteristics of the cars and their price. The first model is:
\[
\texttt{price}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{foreign}_i + \beta_2 \texttt{mpg}_i + \sum_{k=2}^{5} \gamma_k \mathbf{1}\{\texttt{rep78}_i = k\} + \varepsilon_i
\]
The associated code is:
sysuse auto, clear

regress price i.foreign mpg i.rep78, vce(robust)






Tip



The prefix i. declares a variable as categorical. It is required for foreign and rep78 since they are coded as numbers. The option vce(robust) reports heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.


The second model adds an interaction. It assesses whether the association between fuel efficiency and price differs between domestic and foreign cars.
\[
\texttt{price}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{foreign}_i + \beta_2 \texttt{mpg}_i + \beta_3 \texttt{foreign}_i \times \texttt{mpg}_i + \sum_{k=2}^{5} \gamma_k \mathbf{1}\{\texttt{rep78}_i = k\} + \varepsilon_i
\]
regress price i.foreign##c.mpg i.rep78, vce(robust)
The operator ## includes the main effects and the interaction. The operator # includes the interaction only. The prefix c. declares mpg as continuous. Without it, Stata would interact foreign with each value of mpg.

Store and export the results
The estimates are stored with eststo, which can be used in two equivalent ways.
eststo clear

eststo no_inter: regress price i.foreign mpg i.rep78, vce(robust)

regress price i.foreign##c.mpg i.rep78, vce(robust)
eststo inter
The stored estimates remain available until eststo clear or until Stata is closed. They are printed with esttab. The following commands build the final table progressively. Each line adds one option to the previous one.
esttab no_inter inter                                   // Default display
esttab no_inter inter, booktabs                         // LaTeX format
esttab no_inter inter, booktabs se                      // Standard errors instead of t-statistics
esttab no_inter inter, booktabs b(%9.2f) se(%9.2f)      // Number format
esttab no_inter inter, booktabs b(%9.2f) se(%9.2f) ///
    star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01)                       // Significance levels
esttab no_inter inter, booktabs b(%9.2f) se(%9.2f) ///
    star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    indicate("Repair record dummies = *.rep78")         // One line for the dummies
esttab no_inter inter, booktabs b(%9.2f) se(%9.2f) ///
    star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    indicate("Repair record dummies = *.rep78") ///
    label nobaselevels                                  // Variable labels, no base level
The final version adds the statistics, the titles and the notes, and writes the file:
esttab no_inter inter using "$path/output/tables/reg_price.tex", replace ///
    booktabs b(%9.2f) se(%9.2f) ///
    star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    indicate("Repair record dummies = *.rep78") ///
    label nobaselevels ///
    mtitles("Baseline" "Interaction") nonumbers ///
    stats(N r2, fmt(%9.0fc %9.3f) labels("Observations" "R-squared")) ///
    title("Determinants of car prices") ///
    nonotes addnotes("Robust standard errors in parentheses." ///
                     "* p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01")






Tip



The significance levels of the convention in economics are 10%, 5% and 1%. The default levels of esttab are 5%, 1% and 0.1% and should be changed with star().

title: Summary statistics
text:
Advanced users
The package tabout produces complex cross-tabulations directly in LaTeX or Excel. Its documentation is dense and the syntax is demanding, but it is very flexible.

title: Summary statistics
text:
Exercise
To conclude Parts 1 and 2, we combine two sources on the population of the US states. The first one is the built-in census.dta. The second one is an Excel file, nst-est2019-01.xlsx, available in the raw data folder.

Step 1: 1980 data

Set up the do-file. Define two globals: one containing the path and one containing the string 1980 2010, called years
Load census.dta with sysuse and tabulate region. The US census defines four regions: Northeast, North Central (Midwest), South and West
The labels of region are abbreviated. Define a new label with the full names and update the label of region
Using decode region, gen(region_name), create a string variable with the names of the regions
Keep the variables state, region, region_name and pop
Rename pop to pop1980
Save the dataset as $path/temp/census1980.dta



Step 2: 2010 data

Open nst-est2019-01.xlsx with import excel. Only the range A10:B60 is kept, with the option cellrange()
Rename the two columns state and pop2010
The names of the states start with a dot. Remove it with subinstr()
Save the dataset as $path/temp/census2010.dta



Step 3: merge

Clear the memory, open census2010.dta and merge it with census1980.dta, with 1:1 and state as key. Tabulate _merge. What happened?
Some states are named differently in the two datasets. Write a loop over the global years. It opens each dataset, replaces the abbreviations N. by North, S. by South and W. by West, and saves the dataset
Repeat the merge. Inspect the unmatched observations and drop them if they cannot be reconciled



Step 4: statistics

Compute the population change between 1980 and 2010, in percent
Make a table summarising the mean, the standard deviation and the median of this change by region
Reshape the dataset to long format, with two rows per state, one for 1980 and one for 2010



Bonus

Collapse the change by region, computing the mean. Use preserve and restore
Using graph bar var, over(group), make a bar chart of the change by region







NoteSolution





* Step 1
global path "C:/Users/username/courses/2027_eco51423ep"
global years "1980 2010"

sysuse census, clear
tabulate region

label define region_full 1 "Northeast" 2 "North Central" 3 "South" 4 "West"
label values region region_full
decode region, generate(region_name)

keep state region region_name pop
rename pop pop1980
save "$path/temp/census1980.dta", replace

* Step 2
import excel "$path/raw_data/nst-est2019-01.xlsx", cellrange(A10:B60) clear
rename (A B) (state pop2010)
replace state = subinstr(state, ".", "", 1)
save "$path/temp/census2010.dta", replace

* Step 3
foreach y of global years {
    use "$path/temp/census`y'.dta", clear
    replace state = subinstr(state, "N.", "North", 1)
    replace state = subinstr(state, "S.", "South", 1)
    replace state = subinstr(state, "W.", "West", 1)
    save "$path/temp/census`y'.dta", replace
}

use "$path/temp/census2010.dta", clear
isid state
merge 1:1 state using "$path/temp/census1980.dta"
tabulate _merge
list state if _merge != 3
keep if _merge == 3
drop _merge

* Step 4
generate change = (pop2010 - pop1980) / pop1980 * 100
label variable change "Population change 1980-2010 (%)"
tabstat change, by(region_name) statistics(mean sd p50)

reshape long pop, i(state) j(year)

* Bonus
preserve
collapse (mean) change, by(region_name)
graph bar change, over(region_name)
restore
The order of the labels in region_full must follow the numeric coding of region. It should be checked with tabulate region, nolabel.

title: Regression workflow
text: This part presents a standard empirical workflow on panel data: declaring the panel structure, estimating models with fixed effects, choosing the standard errors, and reporting the results. The estimators themselves are covered in the econometrics courses. The objective here is to implement them correctly in Stata.

title: Regression workflow
text:
Data
We use the panel nlswork, an extract of the US National Longitudinal Survey of Young Women. It is available in the Stata web examples. Each row is a woman observed in a given year.
webuse nlswork, clear

describe idcode year ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union age grade race
xtset idcode year          // Declare the panel structure
xtdescribe                 // Participation patterns
summarize ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union
xtset declares the individual identifier and the time variable. It is required for the time-series operators (L., F., D.) and for the commands xt.

title: Regression workflow
text:
Pooled regression
The dependent variable is the logarithm of the hourly wage. The explanatory variables are job tenure, total work experience and union membership.
regress ln_wage tenure ttl_exp i.union

Standard errors
The default standard errors assume homoskedastic and independent errors. Observations of the same individual are correlated over time. The standard errors should then be clustered at the level of the individual.
regress ln_wage tenure ttl_exp i.union, vce(robust)                 // Heteroskedasticity-robust
regress ln_wage tenure ttl_exp i.union, vce(cluster idcode)         // Clustered by individual
The choice of the clustering level follows the sampling design and the assignment of the treatment. The reference on this question is Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2023), “When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?”, Quarterly Journal of Economics.


Interactions and marginal effects
The effect of tenure may differ between union and non-union workers. The command margins computes the predicted wage at chosen values, and marginsplot plots the result.
regress ln_wage c.tenure##i.union c.ttl_exp, vce(cluster idcode)

margins union, at(tenure = (0(5)20))
marginsplot, xtitle("Tenure (years)") ytitle("Predicted log wage") ///
    title("") legend(pos(6) cols(2))

title: Regression workflow
text:
Fixed effects
Individual fixed effects remove all time-invariant characteristics of the individuals, observed or not. Only the within-individual variation identifies the coefficients.

xtreg
xtreg ln_wage tenure ttl_exp i.union, fe vce(cluster idcode)


reghdfe
The command reghdfe absorbs several sets of fixed effects efficiently. The syntax is the same as for regress, with the option absorb().
reghdfe ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union, absorb(idcode) vce(cluster idcode)
reghdfe ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union, absorb(idcode year) vce(cluster idcode)
The second command adds year fixed effects, which capture the shocks common to all individuals. The fixed effects do not appear in the output. They are reported in the table with estadd.






WarningTime-invariant variables



With individual fixed effects, the coefficients of variables that do not vary within individuals, such as race, cannot be estimated. They are absorbed by the fixed effects. Stata omits them and reports it in the output. Variables that evolve in a deterministic way, such as age, are nearly collinear with the combination of individual and year effects.

title: Regression workflow
text:
Report the results
A regression table in an economic paper reports several specifications side by side. The fixed effects are shown with a line “Yes” or “No” at the bottom of the table. The command estadd local adds such a line to the stored estimates.
The order matters. estadd acts on the last estimation, so it is run before eststo.
eststo clear

regress ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union, vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "No"
estadd local year_fe "No"
eststo m1

reghdfe ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union, absorb(idcode) vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "Yes"
estadd local year_fe "No"
eststo m2

reghdfe ln_wage tenure ttl_exp union, absorb(idcode year) vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "Yes"
estadd local year_fe "Yes"
eststo m3

esttab m1 m2 m3 using "$path/output/tables/reg_wage.tex", replace ///
    booktabs b(%9.3f) se(%9.3f) ///
    star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    label nomtitles ///
    mgroups("Log hourly wage", pattern(1 0 0) ///
        prefix(\multicolumn{@span}{c}{) suffix(}) span erepeat(\cmidrule(lr){@span})) ///
    stats(ind_fe year_fe N r2, ///
        fmt(%s %s %9.0fc %9.3f) ///
        labels("Individual fixed effects" "Year fixed effects" "Observations" "R-squared")) ///
    nonotes addnotes("Standard errors clustered by individual in parentheses." ///
                     "* p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01")
The option mgroups() adds a title above the columns. Its syntax is demanding and the block above can be reused as a template. A simpler alternative is mtitles("(1)" "(2)" "(3)").
The coefficients of a variable across specifications are compared with coefplot.
coefplot (m1, label("Pooled")) (m2, label("Individual FE")) (m3, label("Individual and year FE")), ///
    keep(tenure ttl_exp) xline(0, lcolor(red)) ///
    xtitle("Coefficient on log hourly wage") legend(pos(6) cols(3))

title: Regression workflow
section: Beyond the two-way fixed effects model
text:
Beyond the two-way fixed effects model
Difference-in-differences and event-study designs are widely used in applied work. When the treatment is staggered over time, the standard two-way fixed effects estimator can be biased. Several estimators have been proposed and are implemented in user-written packages, among others csdid (Callaway and Sant’Anna), did_multiplegt (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille), eventstudyinteract (Sun and Abraham) and did_imputation (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess). They are not covered in this course.

title: Regression workflow
text:
Exercise






TipExercise



Using nlswork:

Regress ln_wage on tenure and ttl_exp with standard errors clustered by individual
Add the controls age, grade and i.race. Is the coefficient of tenure stable?
Add individual fixed effects with reghdfe. What happens to race? Why is the coefficient of grade identified by few observations only?
Add year fixed effects
Export a table with the four specifications and two lines indicating the fixed effects
Plot the coefficient of tenure across the four specifications









NoteSolution





webuse nlswork, clear
xtset idcode year
eststo clear

regress ln_wage tenure ttl_exp, vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "No"
estadd local year_fe "No"
eststo m1

regress ln_wage tenure ttl_exp age grade i.race, vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "No"
estadd local year_fe "No"
eststo m2

reghdfe ln_wage tenure ttl_exp age grade i.race, absorb(idcode) vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "Yes"
estadd local year_fe "No"
eststo m3

reghdfe ln_wage tenure ttl_exp age grade i.race, absorb(idcode year) vce(cluster idcode)
estadd local ind_fe "Yes"
estadd local year_fe "Yes"
eststo m4

esttab m1 m2 m3 m4 using "$path/output/tables/reg_wage_exercise.tex", replace ///
    booktabs b(%9.3f) se(%9.3f) star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    stats(ind_fe year_fe N r2, fmt(%s %s %9.0fc %9.3f) ///
        labels("Individual fixed effects" "Year fixed effects" "Observations" "R-squared"))

coefplot m1 m2 m3 m4, keep(tenure) xline(0) legend(pos(6) cols(4))
The variable race is constant within individuals and is dropped in the fixed effects specifications. The variable grade varies within individuals for a small number of women only, so its coefficient rests on little variation. In the last specification, age is nearly collinear with the individual and year effects (age is approximately the year minus the year of birth). Its standard error is large and the coefficient is not interpretable.
